newsitem.title: HONG KONG: No upgrade for Telecom NZ despite new govt - Salomon.
newsitem.headline: No upgrade for Telecom NZ despite new govt - Salomon.

text.p: The formation of a centre-right government in New Zealand is good news for Telecom Corp but won't lead to a profit improvement over the next two financial years, Salomon Brothers said on Thursday.

Dan Sherman, vice president of Asia-Pacific Equity Research at Salomon Brothers Hong Kong, said although the new administration had positive implications for New Zealand's largest listed company, he would not be upgrading his earnings forecasts for Telecom.
"What I had thought before is that we would not have much change to the status quo, and all this does is just reinforce that, it ensures that that'll happen," Sherman told Reuters.

Last month, Salomon downgraded its Telecom earnings estimates to NZ$775 million from NZ$815 million for the 1997 year, and to $869 million from $916 million for 1998, on the basis of a slowing economy.

On Tuesday a new government was formed in New Zealand, almost two months after inconclusive elections left the two major parties vying for the support of nationalist New Zealand First. New Zealand First, which held the balance of power, finally decided to join with the incumbent National Party to form a centre-right coalition.
Although National had to make concessions in several key policy areas to secure NZ First's favour, the framework on which New Zealand's free-market reforms have been based remains largely intact.

Sherman said the widening of the central bank's target band for underlying inflation from 0-2 percent to 0-3 percent was not viewed negatively, and could be earnings positive for Telecom by allowing more economic growth.
"Making the target a little bit wider, for all we know that may actually be a little bit better," Sherman said.

But he would be sticking with his previous profit forecasts. "What I had thought before is that they (the new government) would have almost no regulatory change...and all this does is just make that even more solid.
"Probably the real impact is on the macro side, so the real impact should be in what the new government does in terms of interest rates and monetary policy.
"But then again, most of the good things that were done in the New Zealand economy before are going to be kept."
Sherman said Telecom's planned $1 billion share buy-back would drive the company's share price, bolstering stock demand in the short term and improving earnings per share (EPS) thereafter.
"I see that as a second dividend without the tax consequences," Sherman said.
He said Telecom's management was held in high regard by offshore investors and Salomon was still recommending Telecom as a "buy".

"I think that everyone is still willing to go with this management. As you get an upsweep in the economy, which a lot of people are expecting in '97, they're going to look at New Zealand, and the first stock they're going to look at is Telecom," Sherman said.
Telecom shares gained 15 cents to NZ$7.45 when the market opened after the coalition deal was announced, but have since eased back to $7.37 on Thursday.
Ameritech and Bell Atlantic own 49.9 percent of Telecom. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473-4746
